reasoning: Close call, decided on breadth of decision support rather than on the candidate-distinctness test, which came out near-even. DISTINCTNESS AUDIT (the sharpest test): A claims 13 candidates; honest count is ~11 distinct mechanisms, ~10 if you are strict. Two collapses are left standing: #5 'episodic grouping (by session/month)' and #6 'time-bucket browse (week/month/2025)' are the same mechanism — group the list by time so browsing replaces recall — in two costumes; #11 'account-wide index' and #12 'self-serve restore + support console' are a lookup and its completion, and A itself bundles them into a single approach. B presents 20 angle-outputs in Part 3, of which only ~11-12 are distinct (items 1/4/7/15/17/20 are all one temporal-recognition family; 9/10 are both creation-time naming; 13/16 are both resurfacing; 14 and 20 are meta-moves, not ideas) — but B does not present the 20 as its answer. Part 4 is explicitly headed 'Clustering the twenty into seven real candidates' and collapses them to 7, of which 7 are genuinely distinct (creation-time naming / temporal-visual recognition / unified cross-boundary index / identity repair / ambient resurfacing / semantic content retrieval / re-use-over-retrieve). So the honest numbers are A 11-of-13 and B 7-of-7 (from 20 raw). A's larger count is mostly finer slicing of the same territory, not additional territory: the union difference is small, and the one real gap is A's — it has no 're-use over retrieve' idea at all, which is arguably the biggest single escape from the search frame in either document, and it lacks semantic content retrieval (by explicit reasoned exclusion). B does the deduplication itself rather than leaving it for the reader. Net: a tie on this test. FIXATION: A wins this one outright, and it is the clause the user actually wrote ('I can't get past it'). A's Section 1 gives four mechanisms of the fixation itself — inheriting the user's own solution-hypothesis because the verb in the ticket is 'find'; availability (every tool has a search box); 'add search' converting a mushy multi-cause mess into something estimable by Friday; and it being the lowest-blame option, since an option that cannot be wrong also cannot be evaluated. Its tell is excellent: a support ticket means the user already tried, so search most likely converts 'I can't find it' into 'I searched and it's not there', which is a worse ticket. B explains why search is *insufficient* ('a query language for people who already remember the answer' — the sharpest single line in either document) but never explains why this PM keeps returning to it. That is adjacent, not the same, and B fails the expectation. WHY B STILL WINS: the ask was 'need better options', and B is the better options document end to end. It evaluates all seven candidates on four dimensions plus a named validation move each (dry-run the naming heuristic on 200 real projects and read the output yourself; hand-check whether 20 real ticket descriptions contain enough content-words to be resolvable) where A gives only For/Against on three bundles and never evaluates 8 of its 13 candidates individually. B's duds are argued, not asserted — folders and tags 'require exactly the organizational discipline your users have already proven they don't have; you'd be shipping a feature that only serves the users who don't have the problem'. B's metrics are materially better (rate not count, with the reason; % still untitled at day 7 as the leading indicator; zero-result rate as a failure canary; rename-rate as a counter-metric that would catch a bad naming heuristic). B's stress test is a tier above: it attacks its own top recommendation (a confidently wrong auto-name is worse than an honest 'Untitled' because every row now demands evaluation), names its own biggest internal contradiction (recency-first design may be a no-op against the word 'old'), flags survivorship bias in the ticket corpus, and challenges the premise of the brief itself — 'top support complaint' may just be the easiest complaint to articulate, so check whether it correlates with churn. A never challenges the brief. Finally, fit: roughly 35% of A (Sections 5 and 7) is a full technical design of one approach plus a build-approval gate, for a product the document states it has not seen, resting on an admitted guess at Q1. That content is genuinely good — the security surface of the unified index ('a stale index that leaks another account's project title is a security incident that dwarfs the original complaint'), permissions enforced at read time, index rebuild as a first-class tested operation, identity merges always user-confirmed — and it is a real gap in B, which recommends the same unified index and cross-account switching without once mentioning the authorization surface. But it answers a question the user has not reached yet, and A opens with two paragraphs of scope negotiation where B opens with a four-line answer. On expectation count A leads 4-3; per the rubric that is secondary to overall task completion, and on task completion B is ahead.

A.notes: Low padding (~15%). Genuinely wide mechanism coverage — creation-time naming, identity binding, lifecycle transparency, row-level recognition cues, temporal grouping, faceting, query search, proactive resurfacing, spatial persistence, cross-boundary lookup, recovery. No dedup pass of its own; the two collapses are left standing for the reader to notice. Missing entirely: any re-use / 'start from my last one' reframe. Semantic content retrieval is absent by explicit reasoned exclusion, not oversight.

Judged on what B actually proposes, 7 of 7 are structurally distinct. Smaller set than A's, covering nearly the same territory, plus two mechanisms A lacks (semantic content retrieval; re-use-over-retrieve).

distinctness_audit.verdict: Effectively a tie. A surfaces more distinct mechanisms (11 vs 7) but leaves two near-duplicate pairs uncorrected and its extra count is finer slicing of shared territory rather than new territory. B's raw generation list is the more padded artifact but B collapses it honestly and its proposed set has zero waste. Neither side is guilty of the failure this test was designed to catch.
